\[
W_{j,l}(f) = W_j(|f|)\, V\!\left(\frac{\theta(f) - \pi l / L_j}{\pi / L_j}\right),
\quad
V(u) = \cos\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\, \nu(|u|)\big),
\qquad
c_{j,l} = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\big(W_{j,l}\, \mathcal{F} I\big),
\qquad
\hat{I} = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\Big(W_{\text{low}}^2\, \mathcal{F} I + \sum_{j,l} W_{j,l}\, \mathcal{F}\big(\eta(c_{j,l})\big)\Big),
\qquad
L_0 = \text{16}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(f, |f|, \theta(f)\): A frequency in cycles per pixel, its distance from 0 and its angle modulo pi
- \(W_j\): The radial window of band j. Band 0 is the finest.
- \(V\): The angular window, with Meyer's polynomial nu
- \(L_j\): The number of wedges in band j
- \(c_{j,l}\): The coefficients of tile j l
- \(\eta\): Hard thresholding at k sigma times the RMS of the mask

The tiles follow the frequency tiling of the curvelet transform of Candes, Demanet, Donoho and Ying. It has octave bands in radius, each cut into wedges by angle, with more wedges at finer scales. Here the radial windows are W_j^2 = Phi_(j-1)^2 - Phi_j^2. Phi_j is 1 up to a radius of 0.125 / 2^j cycles per pixel and falls smoothly to 0 at twice that radius. The finest band is 1 - Phi_0^2 and the coarse low-pass tile is Phi_(S-1)^2. These squares add up to 1. In each band, L_j wedges are centered at the angles pi l / L_j. V uses Meyer's polynomial nu, so the squares of neighboring wedges also add up to 1. Here theta is the angle of the frequency, modulo pi. L_j halves every second scale toward the coarse end. To remove noise, each tile is filtered, and coefficients below the factor k times sigma times the RMS of the mask are set to 0. That is the standard deviation that white noise of sigma has in the tile. Filtering once more with the mask and adding all tiles rebuilds the image. The tiles are not the curvelets of a curvelet transform, which come with their own sampling and a fast algorithm, so this is a curvelet-inspired filter.
